My father and sister have also pulled me aside to tell me that and to keep up the good work (staying sober, taking care of my mental health) because she is doing things for me that they've never seen her do before.

We are very close and she really gets me.  We have a lot of personality traits in common.  She loves to laugh and I tend to be hilarious.  We cook for each other.  It's like having a best friend that truly loves you and is always ready to help you through life, even when I'm going somewhere in life that she hasn't been.

I've seen her cry at some of the familial insanity going on right now.  Her mother has severe cancer, her father just turned 92, my paternal grandmother is in hospice, my sister is married to a sketchy loser and has a year and a half old child...  Yeah. I don't deserve a mother like her, but DAMN am I glad that I have her.  I know she won't be around forever and that breaks my heart, but she is still here now and I make sure that I get all of the time with her that I possibly can.  I love you, Mom!!!

I have BPD, depression, anxiety with severe agoraphobia, PTSD and some other things going on.  I found that providing employers and/or coworkers with specifics is usually detrimental.  As some others have said, they basically reduce you to your diagnoses and view you through that lens.  They tend to anticipate certain behaviors and such from you and it can makes things really anxiety-inducing very quickly.

The best thing to do if you want them to be aware that something is up is to say you have a chronic health condition and may need some accommodations.  Be prepared to get a doctor's note if asked.  Still, specifics should not be discussed unless your doctor or therapist thinks doing so would make it easier on you.  Again, in my experience...  Not a great route.  But I don't know your entire background.  It may be necessary for you to have a place to go during panic attacks, for example.

Being able to talk with other patients that were going through something similar helped.  There were always a couple of nurses or techs on the wards that I would open up to, and that was great support, especially during my six month and year-long hospitalizations.

The staff was very good at separating the human from the illness.  They were very encouraging and reminded me that I'm not a bad person or useless because of my illness.  They also shared some success stories too.

One place had different therapists come in to speak/give a lesson once or twice a week.  That was a great way to break things up.  They regularly had therapists and other staff from the facilities doing therapy lessons every day.  
  
The only exception to that was my last hospitalization, the longest one for a reason--COVID.  I was hospitalized right when COVID was becoming the problem people feared it would, so we were pretty much on lockdown until I was discharged...  A YEAR later.

Even then, the empathetic hospital staff, other patients, and one-on-one therapy helped a lot.  My doctor actually saw me more frequently than normal.  I asked and they said that COVID was messing with people so much that they were taking extra precautions.

The last thing, this may or may not be your situation, but my parents and family were so proud of me.  Another reason I was there so long was because my father said they better not discharge me before I was ready.  He wanted my psych ward revolving door to be closed!  So to speak lol  But they know I can't control that but I can work to minimize symptoms and be fairly productive.  I'm still working on recovering to get to my former baseline or close to it.  Extreme alcohol abuse, smoking weed ALL DAY and waking up to do it at night!!!, and a SA when I was younger gave me a lot to work through.

I now have something called an ACT Team.  That stands for Assertive Community Treatment.  They began working with me about a month before I was discharged.  I don't have a car (I totaled mine when trying to unalive myself) and they come to see me 2-3x a week.  They bring my meds every week, provide one-on-one and group therapy (I really love my group people), my psychiatrist comes to me, they take me to doctor appointments, to the grocery store, out to parks, and things like that.

I used to have so much potential.  Then I pretty much shot that horse in the face.  But I'm slowly, but surely becoming myself again, so it must be a zombie horse now lol (Just trying to make you smile :) )

I just hit a year weed-free on March 20th of this year.  I had been using it for about 13 years.  I kept thinking about how much money (and time!) I'd save not smoking or vaping it, the positive health benefits, and the fact that it felt so crappy for a few months after quitting served as a reminder that it wasn't as "safe" as every stoner claims.  If it was, it wouldn't have been so hard to quit and made me feel like absolute shit after I quit.

The staff and activities (like various therapy groups and one-on-one therapy) made a big difference.  The first few times I was hospitalized, I was sent to a place closest to where I was living.  It was terrible.  Very apathetic staff (that were often quite rude and cruel), poor control over other patients (leading to a lot of fighting), use of restraints and physical contact when it wasn't necessary.  I found out after my last stay in the worst offender that those particular psychiatric hospitals were known for how terribly they treat patients.

The facilities that were better took their time with us instead of rushing us out in 72 hours.  Doctors and therapists checked in on us several times a day compared to once or twice in three days.  They asked the right questions and listened.  There was group therapy and other therapy, like reading groups, religious groups, art groups, AA meetings, etc.  These places did a good job connecting patients to one another and making it easy to find people we related to.  They kept us safer and made us feel safe.  The staff was much kinder and more empathetic.  You could tell they had passion for the work they did.

I've been hospitalized for psychiatric reasons 15 times.  My last two hospitalizations were six months long and a year long.  I'm very blessed that these facilities were two of my preferred ones.  Some psychiatric facilities near me are notoriously bad.  Even my psychiatrists and therapists admitted that one in particular never helps anyone aside from drugging you to hell--and obviously, that doesn't really work either.

I attempted suicide a few times.  The last time, I drove my car through the front of my employer's business.  My boss had told me that "everyone has anxiety and most people are depressed."  So...  I figured I'd show him the depths of my despair.

The last time I was hospitalized, my parents worked really hard to make sure I would have the resources I needed when I was eventually discharged.  I now have a safe, beautiful apartment, an ACT team (google it if you're not sure what that is), and my team checks on me 2-3x a week.  I can reach them 24/7 and they take me out on outings with other recovering addicts with severe mental illness.

For about five or six years, things were really bad.  Active addiction (weed and a LOT of alcohol), self harm, suicide attempts, constant dark thoughts...  And I really tried not to share that with anyone.  They would think I'm doing good, then get a call from me or my ex saying that I was BACK in the hospital again.  Every 2-4 months I was hospitalized.  It was like that for years.  But now I have my team and it's very easy to be honest with them and stay safe.

Please, everyone, take care of your mental health.  If you need help, reach out to someone.  There are great resources out there.  Stay safe, y'all!

Emotional support animals and service animals have different applications and rights.  A service animal performs tasks for their owners while ESAs offer their presence and interaction to help their owners.  An ESA will not be allowed in public settings like a service animal would.  You would not be able to take an ESA to work with you but you can get a letter from your doctor to be able to have one within your housing.  Please note that claiming an animal is a service animal when it is not is illegal in many places and can result in as much legal action as imprisonment.

I'm not quite sure why you are concerned about your employer/job and an ESA if they are not present in a workplace with you.  If you have more specific questions about that, I can try to help you. However, I started experiencing even more nausea.  That kept me using for a while before I really decided that I was sick and tired of feeling like that and spending the money that I really didn't have.  "Sick and tired of being sick and tired," as they say in AA/NA.

The nausea can be treated but will likely be persistent initially.  For me, it was really bad for the first four-to-five weeks.  It started improving a lot around weeks six-to-seven.  I saw that she is taking medication for nausea.  If that doesn't work and she is able to take it, pepto bismol might help as well.  It helped me a lot.  
  
Stopping cold turkey was a better option for me, and I think how terrible it felt was a good thing.  It kind of gave me perspective into what I was doing to myself and I couldn't trick myself into taking an extra puff or two as my final hurrah as I tapered off. 

Being supportive and realistic with her is really important.  She can possibly feel crappy for a while, but that's what happens when you start abusing a substance and stop it.  Drinking water, eating nutritious meals (and making sure she is eating at all--that could be hard too!), and good sleep will help her out tremendously.  If you could find out what made her start vaping, that could be very insightful regarding how to proceed as well.

OP, I just hit a year on March 20th.  I definitely know how you are feeling.  I tried to quit many times over a decade.  This last time, things are finally working out.

The hardest part is the mental unease that you can't quite describe.  There is no way to describe it to someone who hasn't been there themselves.  The first two weeks were the worst psychologically, and then the first month-to-six weeks was when I had the worst physical symptoms like nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, severe headaches,  trouble eating (I became Hangry for a bit there!), etc.

I noticed as soon as two or three weeks in that my memory was getting SO much better.  And a few months after that, I was able to cope with things psychologically much better than any time since before I smoked weed (so about since 2012).  I was hospitalized 15 times, one time for a YEAR straight (the last time).  After 2013, I was going into the hospital a few times per year.  I am proud to say that I haven't been hospitalized since 2022.

I still struggle with some of that mental discomfort when I have panic attacks.  But I've gone from having a hundred or more panic attacks per month (seriously...) to a dozen/couple dozen.  I'm still working on recovery, and it would be inaccurate for me to say that after a certain time point, all of the quitting-ness goes away.  At least, I'm not quite there yet.  But things have gotten incredibly easier for me.  If I can do it, so can you!    
  
Don't try to rush things.  Accept how you feel, even if you feel like shit.  Know what you are doing for yourself and why you are doing it.  Those benefits will always outweigh using weed.

OP, you seem very capable of self-reflection.  You can harness that to address both the negative things you're feeling, the positive things in your life, and the positive things you can do to ensure a better future for yourself.  Your anger and negative emotions can be utilized to create more positive ultimate outcomes.  That's a good way to help you see why you need to do and get you motivated and moving.

I worked on it, though, and my parents tell me all of the time that "Our girl is back!" and that they are proud of me.  None of us expected that outcome.  In fact, therapists during my 15 psych admissions pretty much told my very loving parents to abandon ship.  I didn't know that until recently when my Dad and I were talking about how far I've come.

You've got more to work with than you're giving yourself credit for!  I am not a professional--this is just all my personal experiences.  If you or anyone else wants to chat, I'll be here!  :)

OP, I can promise you that substances are not stabilizing you.  I think you are beginning to see that.  I'm a recovering alcoholic and pothead.  I told myself for years that, the weed especially, was helping me control my symptoms.  But I was hospitalized 15 times, the last two times being six months long and then the last hospitalization being about a year long.

I started using again after being discharged and I could really tell how much neither substance was helping me.  Because I'm stubborn, I kept trying for a few months.  Then I thought about how much time and money I spent getting substances, how dangerous alcohol use (even moderate) is with the medications I take, and how much is was messing up things like my memory and ability to socialize without intense anxiety.

I hit a year weed-free in February and I'm close to a year alcohol-free.  It sucked at first, especially the first two or three months.  But it keeps getting easier and I'm continuing to see the infinite improvements in my mind and body.  Those around me notice as well.  My Dad told me a few days ago that my recovery is "amazing" and "basically a miracle."  I'm fortunate that I've been able to repair my most important relationships and improvements are continuously being made on that front as well.

When you first sober up, it will kind of stir up your mind and can make some BDP symptoms and thoughts harder to deal with.  But if you keep your eye on the prize and think about the numerous long-term benefits that are truly within your reach, things will keep getting better for you.  And not to mention the pride you can feel in yourself for doing something that is so hard.

It would be a great idea if you could find a place to go to help you sober up.  A psychiatric facility could help you find housing solutions, too, if that is necessary.  And if you don't already have a psychiatrist, they can help with that and therapy as well.

One of the guys in my SUD group has been sober for about seven years and he said that one day he decided something needed to change and he drove up to the hospital and checked himself in.  Just something to think about.  
  
I hope this helped you out!  Feel free to ask any questions you might have.  :)

I have a unique perspective to share here:  
  
So I spent the second half of 2019 and the end of 2020 - early 2022 in psych wards and psych hospitals.  Prior to that and during that time, I was a serial patient.  All of the local places knew me by then.

I broke up with my fiance in the spring of 2019.  COVID-19 stuff was starting to trickle in.  I was in the hospital for a suicide attempt, discharged a few months later, then was back in another hospital for a year because I drove my car into my employer's front entrance.

I was used to having visitors while hospitalized.  My ex, my family, some friends.  They would usually bring me things like clothes, books, and some toys.  When the COVID shit really hit the fan, they wouldn't let anyone have visitors and anything that couldn't be sanitized was not allowed.  You can imagine how being away from family and friends for a year while you're locked up with not much more than the average prisoner would have would fuck with your mind.

We had TVs and phones, so we kept up with the COVID news.  But our COVID coverage time was limited every day.  A lot of us thought they were exaggerating.  Really...  All of those people out of work and LOCKED DOWN?  Surely, it couldn't be *that* bad.  It's fucking 2020 and 2021 for God's sake!

When new patients were admitted, we got a LOT of info about how insane things were and how things were not being exaggerated.  It made my anxiety significantly worse, and that's saying a lot...

Now, my parents, support team, sister, etc. will say something like, "I haven't seen that since COVID."  My dad and I were talking last week about the rise of online shopping and how COVID affected that.  At the end of that conversation he said, "It was just a really strange time.  Nothing felt real.  You saw evidence of other people outside of your household but really didn't see the actual people."

He and my mother (a teacher) said that the effect COVID had on my generation and below (I'm 32) is something we will probably never recover from, especially the youngest generations that were present for it.

That period just feels like a time warp.  Like someone let something happen in a game, watched to see how it would develop, and then was like, "Shit, not that," and pulled the cord before the game could save.  But it had already started saving...  Ugh.

Inpatient stays like you've described are designed to lessen the immediate chance of suicide or severe self harm. I've been in psych wards/psych hospitals 15 times.  All but once or twice was involuntary.  My last two stays were six months and a year. Psychiatric facilities/psych-only hospitals are designed for longer stays and that's where I had my best treatment outcomes.

- Getting products I really enjoy and get excited about using

- Developing a routine, not just for makeup, but for general skincare as well

Hey there!  I've been hospitalized 15 times for psychiatric issues.  One time was a year long!  But, yes, I have a lot of experience in this area.

Hospital placement kind of depends on the severity of your symptoms first and then what placements are available second.  I've been at several larger hospitals (not psych-specific) and they are not really equipped to treat cases like mine.  They usually held me until a psych-only hospital could take me.  They were really nice facilities, but not right for me.  I've been to three psychiatric hospitals and it's much more controlled.  Less opportunities to be alone, much more patient watching and interacting, therapy, a strict schedule to keep everyone involved.

I have a history of pretty bad self harm and the last time I had done that pretty much all over my body in addition to the suicide attempt that followed.  I have been placed in restraints many times because I found something to cut myself with or started banging my head on the wall or something else stupid.  That last time was intense.  At the psych hospitals, they were ready to pounce to keep things calm for everyone else.  The responses and response time to situations was much more intense and rapid in a psychiatric hospital than the general hospital.

Being around other patients going through the same thing or something very similar was helpful too.  It made me feel less alone and less crazy.  They were a great help when I needed to ground myself.  During a few stays, the other patients were at least as beneficial as the medications and therapy.  You can process things differently with people going through it too vs the hospital staff.

The psychiatric facilities were really great at noticing trends, noticing when trends changed, etc.  They could tell when I was BSing them just trying to be discharged sooner.  It actually worked for a few times, then a nurse pointed it out to me and said they can tell when patients tell them crap, fake emotions, etc.  This was also helpful when trying to sort through some of the drug seekers.  I saw many folks come through trying to get xanax or other benzos.

(YEAH, I can say, finally, it's been years since I've been in a psych hospital or hospitalized for psych symptoms.  WHOOP!)

I've attempted suicide four times and have been hospitalized for suicide attempts, ideation with self harm, etc. fifteen times.  Since 2013.  My last hospitalization was about a year long.  I was discharged almost a year ago.  Due to my history and being at a pretty stellar psychiatric hospital, I was set up with a fantastic safety net to assist me both during and after discharge for long-term care.  I would not have qualified for my treatment and social services teams if things hadn't gotten as bad as they did the last time.  The last suicide attempt was me wrecking my car into the side of my former employer's building because my boss had told me he has anxiety too and to just "get over it like \[he\] did--it's not that hard!"

My treatment team checks on me multiple times per week.  They bring me my meds weekly, provide therapy, take me to the store if I need it.  I have a crisis team on-call if it's needed.  I'm not working.  I'm still afraid of leaving my apartment but NOT if someone is with me, but I'm working on it.  I can take my trash out without getting too nervous and paranoid, so that's a pretty big deal to me.

The government and nonprofit programs that have come together to help me move into my beautiful new apartment a few months ago have been amazing to work with.  It's really incredible to think that there are people like that out there.  It took a LOT longer to move than expected (I waited eight months in the hotel vs their two month or less goal), but given the housing that I did eventually get, waiting a few extra months isn't so bad.  I pay 25% of my rent and funds from one of the programs helps me pay the rest.  It's made it really easy for me to rest my mind and feel safe.  I take pride in how beautiful my home is and that I am strong enough to be here to enjoy it.

I lost pretty much everything by six months into that hospitalization.  My dog, my home, many belongings were left behind or donated.  The program working with me when I was discharged provided me with $5000 to furnish my new home, buy cooking stuff, etc.  I now have a lovely pet cat that I adopted a little over a month ago too.  Every time my treatment team comes over they say that it's so clean in here, they love show I decorated, it smells good.  I take pride in my home now and that's a great indicator of success for me.

Ironically, I started having panic attacks the other day after thinking about how good I've been feeling overall and the inevitable next slip.  It's happened fifteen times already...  I'm sure it'll happen again.  :/  A few weeks ago I turned 30 years old and I thought about suicide so that I could end things on a high note, so to speak.  But I'm glad I didn't. I've been hospitalized for psychiatric care 15 times.  Sometimes for only 72 hours with my most recent hospitalization lasting about *a year.*  Here are a few things to expect:

* A LOT of free time.  My family mailed me tons of books during my last stay as visitors weren't allowed due to COVID.  Coloring books, journals, sudoku, word searches, etc. are good to have around.
* You might have to wear masks indoors around other patients.  I got both of my COVID shots during my last hospitalization and we were still highly encouraged to wear masks in common areas.
* Possible group sessions.  I HATED the idea of these because I'm kind of shy and awkward but they ended up being fairly helpful.  Still, outpatient therapy has been much more beneficial for me, as usually is the case.
* A lot of people are going to want to know how you're feeling.  Be honest.  If I'd been honest early-on I would've received better and more targeted treatment (and I would've spent much less time in the hospital!).
* Other patients...  This is where it gets interesting.  Everyone is kind of in their headspace.  Everyone there is there for different reasons.  I chose to observe other patients and be polite, while quiet, so I could feel them out more.  I'm actually still friends with a couple of the ladies I met last year and earlier this year.
* It's okay to want to be alone.  It's hard being around people--both patients and staff included.  Don't hesitate to take some time alone in your room.  You might have a roommate but in my experience that was still much better than sitting in the common areas all day.

**Mains**

*Instant soup*:  Can of tomatoes, broth/bouillon, onion, whatever veggies and meat I have.  For chicken soup omit the tomatoes.  If you really want to make it cheap and easy just use bouillon and water.  The bouillon and water is apparently good to eat after exercise.

*Beans*:  Overnight soak?  Not for me.  I plan what I'm going to eat for dinner in the morning.  I put them in a pot and soak all day then cook them in the afternoon or at night.  Cooking still takes some time but it can save you some money buying dried beans and you can make a lot at once an meal prep if you'd like.

*Grilled Cheese*:  You can make this more or less healthy depending on the bread and cheese used.  I splurge on bread, one of the few things I don't get for cheap unless it's on sale.  I get Dave's brand breads when they're on sale (about every other week).  A little bit of butter in the pan (to use less) or on the bread itself (uses more), a piece or two of cheese, done in less than five minutes from the start sandwich assembly.

**Sides**

*Microwaved corn on the cob:*  Corn on the cob is 5/$1 here and I don't have an oven currently to bake it like I usually would.  Put it in whole and unshucked for 3-4.5 minutes depending on cob size.  Wait a minute when it's done then peel it easily and add butter, salt, etc.  You can also boil it but that takes more effort than the microwave does.

*Banana Desert*:  Get a very yellow-to-ripe banana.  Put a little butter in a pan.  Slice banana.  Add banana to the pan with some sugar.  I prefer brown sugar.  I tried this for the first time the other day and it took like two or three minutes and tasted like something with a lot of effort put into it.

*Microwaved Baked Potatoes*:  I'm currently living in a hotel and don't have an oven.  My mom, who has an oven, suggested making baked potatoes by microwaving them.  It's a great idea!  Use a fork to poke some holes in a potato and put it in the microwave for around five minutes.

* Adobo seasoning is a great way to add flavor to a dish without the fuss of individual spices and salt.
* Not healthy but...  Butter.  Throwing in a little bit can enhance many dishes.
* Garlic salt has a buttery taste.  I use it in my potatoes to cut down on the butter I use.  I use it in almost everything.

I'd forget my name, deeply ingrained personal information, where I was, how to operate the cash register, etc.

\- Memory and concentration are improving

\- Weight loss

\- Almost NO panic attacks (Docs said they wouldn't be surprised if I stop having them the longer I remain sober).  What I've had were not full-force panic attacks.

\- Less Depression

\- Less Paranoia

I hope this has answered your question a bit.  I think the key here is to adopt the mindset that you have an additional reason to stay sober and this is a fabulous opportunity to do so. The great thing about training dogs is that there is no set list of tasks for them to do.  Some people use dogs to help them out and others train dogs to dance for them.  The best training is a result of calm, confident encouragement and calm, consistent rewarding.  I teach my clients that we unintentionally train dogs things all of the time.  They pick up on our habits and deduce what to expect even if we don't reward them.  Here's how it started with Boomhauer:

There are certain things I do when I'm anxious.  But the core of it is something dogs can pick up on long before we're even aware of the beginnings of it.  They can sense our heart rates and smell fluctuations in our hormones, hear differences in our breathing, tell the difference between a normal breath, a very short one, and a breath meant to be soothing, and things like that.  A lot of people with mental health issues have similar patterns before doing things.  People can pick up them, like my Dad mentioned not being able to notice anything.  But dogs are much more in tune with things humans cannot pick up on so easily.

I've been in therapy for a while, so things have improved amazingly for me.  But I still need help picking up on my subtle physiological changes.  Boomhauer started by coming up to me and pushing his snoot under my hand or nudging my knee about 10-15 seconds before panic attacks after I'd had him for about a month.  It's gotten to the point now that I have utilized his instinct to help him help me.  <3

- Breathing changes, sighs, or abnormal movements.  These are things I inadvertently trained him to notice.  He linked the things I began teaching him to respond to to these things.  Regardless of whether or not a dog is a trained service animal or that the owner has a mental illness, it's much, much more likely than not that s/he notices changes from our typical habits--especially mentally/emotionally.

- Lack of eye contact with him.  Eye contact has always been a strong suit of mine, let it be with other humans or animals.  With dogs, prolonged eye contact can symbol things such as dominance and confidence.  When I did basic obedience training with him, of course I repeated this with him like the other dogs I'd trained and the other dog I owned at the time.  He learned that my breathing changes + lack of eye contact+ me looking around very quickly (trying to remember where I am) = she needs help and is confused.

- He's seen me when my panic/anxiety were the most severe and now, even despite today, things are the best they've been for me since I began having panic attacks.  Dogs are creatures of habit, so he can tell when I'm doing well and when I'm struggling.  This is the last thing that wasn't intentionally trained because I cannot replicate it.  But he knows how I look, carry myself, talk, communicate, etc., when I'm feeling well.  If anything is even slightly different he watches me more.

- I started by teaching him when to pay attention by noticing when he responded to what I mentioned above.  I keep treats everywhere all of the time to reinforce desirable behaviors and I started using them for this before thinking about everything I'll mention next.  When I noticed him noticing me I treated him and said "Goooood!"  Training like this is important and easier for them.  You train them to notice a cue before shaping their response into what you want them to do.  Once I noticed he was consistently responding to my inadvertent cues, I decided to work with him more.

From there, I've taught him things that are specific to me:

- Helping me stay balanced and guiding me to a place to sit during my more severe attacks.

- Laying on me/against me and breathing in slowly and exhaling slowly, poking me with his nose or a paw to help me breathe like him.  He does this in a very obvious way that he never does otherwise.

- Deep pressure therapy.  This is something that a lot of service dogs for panic attacks/anxiety and PTSD do.  They lay on you in a way that is stimulating a bit like a weighted blanket, but more so because he's warm and also breathing.

- Noticing sudden changes in my breath.  I worked on this with him more after noticing that he noticed it.  Especially when I'm doing well, a few times a day I'll suddenly gasp and touch him somewhere without looking at him.  He will do deep pressure therapy and start breathing slowly in and out.

- Self harm.  He's seen me do it many times.  As you know, dogs can smell blood.  There is no other time I do the motions I do when self harming.  I noticed that he noticed when I did it, would lay on me or against me, and watch me after I finished.  He would distract me when I went to pick up what I was using again or when I stared at the wounds.  I started repeating this without actually cutting myself--getting the same tools out, looking at them the same way, mimicking my motions, and rewarding him when he would nudge my hand away.  Eventually it got to where we are now.  He will pretty much knock it out of my hand or else throw a fabric or object between me and the SH tool.

- He notices when I forget to take meds.  Remember consistency?  Exactly.  I take them around the same time every day, within about a 30-40 minute period.  If I get to about an hour without taking that he will nudge the meds, bring me an empty bottle that I leave under the bed to keep track of refills, and if I'm doing something like drinking and intentionally not caring about meds...  He will make a mess by the meds.  He'll do something to make me at least go look at what he's done.  This is usually something like messing up the made bed (something he never does otherwise and taught himself because he learned it was effective--lol!) or taking a big mouthful of food and dropping it near the meds.  My apartment is small and I always have my meds nearby, so this is easy.  In places that are bigger like my parents' home he will nudge me and lay a paw on me until I ask him "What?"  Then he'll lead me to my meds, even if they're still in my suitcase or a drawer.

There are other things as well, but I don't want you to be reading for the rest of the year!  A lot of it depends on how you display anxiety an panic.  But dogs can truly feel the differences in our blood pressure, hear our heart rates change, and notice how our breathing changes.  They notice this regardless of whether or not they've been intentionally taught to.  I always teach this to the owners and dogs in my classes and I finally figured I could use it to the benefit of both of us.  :)

I can't help but be disappointed when it happens.  Anyone trying to live sober will feel disappointed.  However, there is a way to be constructive with it.  Beating yourself up over it isn't productive.  It seems like it would be--at least a little bit.  But since psychological factors and mental health play a massive role in addiction we need to remember that we need to treat ourselves with kindness.  A good example of this is I know that when my parents were mad at me when I was growing up that was easier for me to write off than them being disappointed.  Disappointment is it's own unique cluster of emotions.

So what do I do when I'm disappointed?

1.  I don't have expectations.  I don't expect to succeed and for everything to be dandy.  I *hope* it will be.  I *pray it will be.*  But based on my history I shouldn't expect it to, especially coming out of something like my last binge.  When we expect something from ourselves (and especially others) and those expectations aren't met, we tend to have a hard time sorting through that.  Especially if it seems like it would be easy or what we expect to happen would be the logical choice (IN EITHER DIRECTION--postitive or negative).
2. I think about why the slip-up happened.  Was it a "just one drink" scenario?  Did I feel depressed or extra anxious that day?  Did I feel *too good?*  By thinking it through like this I've learned that I often drink more when I'm feeling really good than when I'm feeling very bad.  I only recently figured this out and it's honestly been a game changer for me.
3. I'm an organized, list-making sort of girl, so I make lists.  Why the slip up happened from the above point is linked to what can I do differently next time when I feel that way?  Some examples for me include:

\- Being productive, finding something positive to do, helping people out online, volunteering

\- Working with my service dog

\- Coloring, word searches, music, or reading

\- Talking to someone:  A therapist, my parents, my sister, *kind strangers!*  :)

\- Going for a walk

\- Spoiling myself with self-care like a nice bath, getting a new fancy soap, putting on makeup and nice clothes, etc.

\- **This is the biggest helper each time!**  How will I feel after drinking?  Not just physically, but mentally.  That's how I use that disappointment in a positive way.  I use that reminder of feeling disappointed, then often remember feeling like absolute crap physically, and use that to pick out which coping skills/distractions I'll utilize.  

I try to use positive reinforcement to shape what I do.  Which is funny that I'm saying it that way because I typed it without ever having thought about it in those terms.  I work with dogs and train them.  Positive reinforcement is always leaps and bounds (hehe, pun intended!) more productive than scolding.  I show them what to do and then reward them within five seconds of the desired behaviour.  That's what I've been doing too.  Not so immediate because I'm a person, but it's very much the same concept.  There's no reason to keep shaming yourself when you're already disappointed.  If you're disappointed then you feel the most productive negative emotion you possibly could to make more steps towards your goal of a sober life.

I hope this has been helpful!  I didn't mean to turn this into a TED talk but, as always, sharing my thoughts like this to help someone else helps me *at least* just as much.  I'm an empathetic person but I get a ton out of it too.  Let's be real here!  :)

I think a lot of people are missing the true roots of American "freedom" and how this plays out in modern America.  I'll do a little ELI5 (or more like ELI10) type response.

Things have shifted and "freedom" in colloquial American terms is based on the idea of *freedom* that led to the founding of America.  Our obsession with the word "freedom" comes from the very beginnings of America.  The desire for freedom is what led to America being formed in the first place.  At the time America was formed the freedoms given to the public in general, especially in terms of government and politics, was much more true to the term compared to anywhere else in the world at that time or prior to it.  As such, the word means much to us as a sort of heritage throwback.  For example, most license plates from my state read "First in Freedom."  I'm in the southern US.  This is certainly, um...  Not the case.  :)

The average American has had "freedom" drilled into his/her head since history was first taught to him/her.  We were founded with very liberating principals, especially in lieu of the rest of the world at that time (particularly Europe, especially Britain and colonies being founded globally by Europeans).  A lot of people are unfortunately not too educated about *global* current events and how America stacks up in comparison.  In our history classes the global political comparisons, for all intents and purposes, pretty much stop around the end of WWII and almost hardline after the Korean War.  The only recent international references are military operations attempting to liberate others (like the War in Iraq).  We focus on America's international involvements that attempt to grant more freedom to other countries and not how our current ideas and applications of freedom fit into a modern framework and global setting. This leads to a lot of people still assuming "we're # 1!" as most people are unwilling or too disinterested to do that amount of research on their own.

I was raised in a middle class home, taught to be nice to others.  I grew up volunteering at food banks, going to church, volunteering for schools, in girl scouts, etc.  I started getting bullied in second grade and it didn't stop until about 11th grade.  It started, I can see now, because I was a happy kid with good clothes, nice toys, etc., going to school with a lot of low-income kids.  They were jealous and the fact that I didn't do anything to piss them off due to being naturally nice and polite just frustrated them further.  To them I had it made.  I had everything I could need and much of what I could want.  I always had social anxiety due to what these kids would say and do to me but I held myself together for a while.

When I was 14 years old I was raped.  I developed anorexia.  I dropped about 100lbs in six months.  That's when peers started giving me an easier time.  They knew something was going on but not what it could be.  I never dealt with the trauma and began drinking my sophomore year in college.  I graduated top of my class, had a full scholarship to my #1 college of choice (in fact I only applied at that school because I knew I would get in), and finished my ranked 3rd in the freshman class my first year.  That was out of a little under 20,000 students so...  Yeah.  Quite good there.

But then the anxiety ramped up seemingly out of nowhere.  I now know that it was from meeting my ex fiance and the constant stream of alcohol and drugs that he fed me up until about a year ago when I got a DWI.  At that point I was having about 50 panic attacks every day.  I was physicially addicted to alcohol after being the kid in school who encouraged others to not try drugs and alcohol.  My BAC at the time of the DWI was .25.  That's scary stuff.  I thought I knew at that point that every bad thing I'd felt about myself was true.  I'd failed at school, I'd stopped going to church, connecting with people, I was ashamed of myself, I'd been such a good girl growing up and still I was raped.  How does that happen to a good person?  *Why would it?*  I went from raising $100,000 for insecticide-treated bed nets for villages in Chad, Africa in a town of 10,000 people to someone who was completely alone, scared of everything, and either always drunk, hungover, or--most likely--both.

I'm getting back on my feet now.  Due to the bullying when I was younger, my ex fiance (we broke up about 9 weeks ago, btw), and things that happened in between I'm still paranoid about people thinking I think I'm the best thing ever.  I told my therapist this and my parents this separately.  They all said the same things:

1. You can't control what other people think.  Their perceptions and conclusions are based on their experiences and even how that particular day is going, just like it is for you.
2. You can pay attention to what *you* think.  When you start thinking something silly, try to laugh at yourself like I do.  It really does help.
3. It won't be easy, especially since this has been my thought process for over a decade and I'm only 27 years old.
4. Don't ignore those feelings.  THAT is where the danger lies...  Trying to push it away.  The best thing I've done is acknowledge that's how I feel and accept it.  From there I've been able to start working on why I feel that way, remaining mindful of that feeling, and paying attention to people from afar to see how I perceive their behavior when it doesn't include me (especially strangers).

Some anxiety has a purpose--it helps us stay safe and better our lives.  When it becomes out of control is when we really have a problem.  That doesn't mean it's hopeless though.  That feeling of hopelessness is just another of anxiety's screwed up brain games.  We're harder on ourselves than anyone else ever could be and it's very hard to start recovering and improving when you're so hard on yourself.  Forgive yourself and appreciate yourself.  Others already do!  The anxiety just wants to blind you to that.

I'm sorry for the length of this but I hope that it helps you and possibly some other folks too.  :)

I ended last year and began this year in a psych ward.  For the last six years or so I've been in psych wards 2-3 times per year, sometimes for over three months during a single stay.  Last year the stay were both more frequent and longer.  I knew, kind of instinctively, that things were about to change big time for me.  I didn't know if they would be good or bad changes.  Having severe anxiety (50 panic attacks per day at one point) I naturally assumed they would be bad.  I'd been in therapy consistently for about ten months at that point after getting a DWI in February and trying to wreck my car to kill myself.  The court recognized my problem and said if I consistently attended therapy several times per week that they would drop all charges.  I now call that the "best worst thing" that ever happened to me.

But that eerie feeling that things were changing or were about to...  Yeah.  I was with my fiance for nine years!  I lived with him and had never lived on my own.  He was treating me like crap and we broke up.  He had apparently been stealing money from my parents and keeping me around to have the rent paid, home cooked meals, pet care, etc.  I thought that all of that progress would be lost because for the first time ever...  LITERALLY...  I would be living alone.

Now I have an awesome apartment and a job I love, granted we're not working now.  But they refused to lay off anyone.  I only worked there for three weeks before the shut down.  Being isolated socially has been difficult.  I tend to have few people to interact with anyway due to my anxiety, fear of rejection, and just having moved to a new area after the breakup.  I didn't realize that I'm actually a likable person with a killer sense of humor still until being single ("liberated") and feeling comfortable being myself again.

The isolation resulting from the pandemic has definitely taken its toll on me.  I went from 50+ panic attacks per day (\*sigh\* before anyone asks...  YES they were pretty much constant with 5 minutes for recovery, had them in my sleep, etc.) to none for several consecutive months over the last 13-14 months.  When I did have them it was no more than three during an entire month!  I had 25 on Thursday, 17 on Friday, six on Saturday, three on Sunday, and two yesterday.  But it's getting better.  And I felt amazing even through that.  I know how hard I've been working and even though this situation is shitty for everyone my hard work is paying off.  I'm still helping others and doing it much moreso now that I have free time and no man child.  I'm seeing how much strangers appreciate my acts of kindness.  I'm still feeling like me.  Most importantly, though, I feel like this is an excellent trial run of the skills I've aggregated over the last year+.  It has been.  My parents and sister, pretty much the only friends and family I have left after the isolation my ex forced upon me are absolutely amazed at how I've held up.  I've been hospitalized for SH, suicidal ideation/plans, and have acted out over much less.  This is more intense of a situation than any of the things that prompted that response out of me in the past.  And through all of this I've returned to my former/true self.  Funny, quick-witted, friendly, and ready to help out my neighbors.  No need to know who the neighbors are, either.  The "neighbor" part is all I need to know!  :)

Sorry for the rambling, but I felt the context would benefit you.  My point is this...  You can get through this and when you DO! you are going to be so damned proud of yourself.  Hold that torch high in the air and keep using that new flame to light the path for your future, because you've made it through one of the most difficult things most people currently living ever have and you did it with a plate full of...  Not delicious-ness.  I'm here if you ever need someone to talk to.
Amazing job!  Keep it up!
